title: A spring Pacific SST contrast gave no clear added winter ENSO forecast gain in 1982-2025
abstract: We tested whether a spring east-to-west Pacific sea surface temperature contrast improves next-winter ENSO forecasts beyond the central Pacific level and its recent change. We used NOAA CPC ERSSTv5 monthly anomalies and 44 time-ordered forecasts for target winters 1982-2025. Adding MAM Nino 3 minus Nino 4 cut mean squared error by 17.14%. The conditional 95% five-year block interval was -5.02% to +36.48%. Mean absolute error fell from 0.7586 to 0.6726 C. The added skill was 33.75% in 1982-2003 and -1.11% in 2004-2025. Last-30-year training and time-trend checks also left the full-period gain uncertain. A planned JJA check had 13.06% higher mean squared error. The evidence does not establish a reliable added spring forecast gain or a physical cause. This is a benchmark of a known method class. Final data versions, a fixed reference period, 44 winters and conditional uncertainty limit inference. Code, monthly inputs, all forecasts, source hashes, an arithmetic audit, an exact repeat check and a figure are included.

display.caption: Added winter forecast skill from the Pacific contrast, with conditional 95% five-year block intervals. Positive skill means lower mean squared error than the level-change model. The cumulative loss difference shows when the spring model gained or lost accuracy.

citations.reason: Published spring-change evidence sets the stronger baseline. We add a spatial contrast. Source observations overlap; this is not independent confirmation.
ENSO-CLIPER uses levels, trends and several Pacific indices. This study tests an added spatial term in a small fixed model.
Prior work on indices of ENSO evolution and east-to-west temperature patterns. Our contrast differs from the Trans-Nino Index.
Shared CPC ERSSTv5 monthly Nino region snapshot; exact source hash and input values are preserved.
Public-domain terms and attribution for NOAA/NWS data.
